posts.title: Five questions to ask before you write a three-year plan
posts.excerpt: Most plans fail before the first spreadsheet is opened. These five questions keep a leadership team honest about what it is really deciding.
posts.content:
Every autumn, leadership teams start the same ritual: a template goes out, departments fill in their numbers, and three months later a plan arrives that nobody quite believes. The problem is rarely the spreadsheet. It is the questions nobody asked before opening it.

1. What will we stop doing?

A plan that only adds is a wish list. Agree on at least one product, customer group or activity you will deliberately shrink. It frees money and attention, and it tells everyone the plan is serious.

2. Which two numbers will tell us we are winning?

Not twenty KPIs — two. One should be about customers (retention, share of wallet, net revenue per account) and one about how efficiently you serve them.

3. Who owns each priority by name?

Shared ownership is no ownership. Every priority needs one person who reports on it every month and has the budget to act.

If a priority does not have a name and a number next to it, it is not a priority. It is a hope.

Margaret Okafor, Managing Partner

4. What has to be true for this to work?

List the assumptions — market growth, hiring, prices — and decide how you will check them each quarter. Plans break on assumptions far more often than on execution.

5. What will we tell the organisation?

If you cannot explain the plan on one page to a team leader, it is not finished. Write that page first, and let the spreadsheet follow.

posts.title: Closing the books in five days: what actually changes
posts.excerpt: A faster month-end close is not about working nights. It is about fewer handovers, earlier cut-offs and agreeing what “good enough” means.
posts.content:
Finance teams that close in five working days are not staffed with heroes. They have simply removed the work that does not need to happen in the first week of the month.

Move work before day one

Accruals, reconciliations of stable accounts and most intercompany matching can be done in the last week of the previous month. That alone typically removes two days.

Agree materiality up front

Chasing a £200 difference on day four is a choice. Set thresholds with the CFO and the auditors, and document them.

  • A single close calendar, owned by one person
  • Daily 15-minute stand-ups during close week
  • Standard journal templates with built-in checks
  • A post-close review of what slipped and why

The benefit is not only speed. Managers get numbers while they can still act on them, and the finance team gets its evenings back.

posts.title: The weekly operations review your managers will not dread
posts.excerpt: A good weekly review takes 45 minutes, looks forward rather than back, and ends with named actions. Here is the agenda we use with clients.
posts.content:
Most weekly meetings are status updates in disguise. People read numbers aloud that everyone could have read alone, and the hard conversations are left for later.

The 45-minute agenda

  1. Five minutes: safety and customer escalations
  2. Ten minutes: the two headline numbers against target
  3. Twenty minutes: the one or two issues that need a decision
  4. Ten minutes: actions, owners and dates read back aloud

The dashboard is circulated the afternoon before. If nobody has questions about a number, it is not discussed.

The point of the meeting is the decision, not the data.

After six weeks, teams usually find they need fewer other meetings, because issues are surfaced and settled in one predictable place.

posts.title: Cost reduction without cutting the things customers notice
posts.excerpt: Across-the-board cuts are quick to announce and slow to recover from. A customer-led approach protects growth while still finding real savings.
posts.content:
When margins tighten, the reflex is a 10% cut across every budget. It feels fair, and it is almost always wrong: it trims the things customers value as much as the things they never see.

Start from the customer, not the cost centre

Map what your best customers actually pay for — delivery speed, product range, a named account manager — and protect it. Everything else is a candidate.

Look at complexity first

Long-tail products, custom pricing and one-off processes carry hidden costs. Simplifying them often saves more than any headcount reduction, with less damage.

  • Rationalise slow-moving product lines
  • Standardise payment and delivery terms
  • Consolidate suppliers in non-core categories
  • Automate the reports nobody reads, then stop them

Done well, a cost programme leaves the company simpler and faster, not just smaller.

posts.title: What a good board pack looks like in 2026
posts.excerpt: Shorter, earlier and organised around decisions. How the best mid-market boards are rethinking the papers they read every month.
posts.content:
Board packs keep growing. Directors receive 120 pages two days before the meeting and spend most of the session asking what page three means.

Lead with the decisions

The first page should list the two or three decisions the board is being asked to make, with a recommendation and the alternatives considered.

Keep the numbers to one spread

A single page of financial and operational indicators, with commentary only where results differ from the plan, is enough for most meetings.

A board pack is a tool for deciding, not a record of everything that happened.

Send it a full week ahead. Directors who have time to read will bring better questions — and shorter meetings.
